newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade gap shrinks in October, but not with Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade gap shrinks in October, but not with Japan.

text.p: Record exports helped shrink the U.S. trade gap dramatically in October, the Commerce Department said Thursday, largely overshadowing mounting bilateral deficits with Japan and China.
The deficit contracted 30.2 percent to $7.99 billion from a revised $11.44 billion in September -- the lowest monthly shortfall in seven months since $7.87 billion in March.
Exports of all types of goods and services grew 4.2 percent in October to a record $71.74 billion, while total imports declined 0.7 percent to $79.72 billion.
Analysts noted special factors were at work that not only helped bring the monthly deficit down much more sharply than anticipated but that also were unlikely to be repeated.

Foreign sales of American-made commercial aircraft hit a 2-1/2-year peak in October while imports of cars and parts tumbled $1 billion, primarily because of a strike in Canada against General Motors Corp. that has since been settled.

"The 30 percent monthly improvement is clearly overstated because of these special factors," said economist Sung Won Sohn of Norwest Corp. in Minneapolis, adding the prospects were for a deterioration in the trade picture ahead.

"Over the next few months the strong dollar is going to play havoc with trade," Sohn warned, "My other major concern is oil because demand is going up, the price is going up, inventories are low and we'll be importing more of it."
The cost of imported crude petroleum rose to $4.81 billion in October from $4.77 billion in September, even though the volume of barrels imported was down.
The reason was that the price per barrel of imported crude climbed to $21.38 -- the highest since January 1991 during the Gulf War against Iraq -- from $20.02 in September.

Some analysts noted the U.S. economy was expanding at a steady, moderate pace that drew in imports while its key trade partners like Japan and Western Europe were mired in slow growth that made them a poor export market.

"Large trade deficits will persist until the economies of our trading partners begin to match U.S. performance, and the dollar is allowed to settle at a rate determined by market forces rather than foreign intervention," said Marino Marcich, director of international investment for the National Association of Manufacturers.

In another report Thursday, a survey of businesses in the region served by the Philadelphia Federal Reserve bank showed a decline in the business conditions index, suggesting a potential December slowdown.

The index declined 2.2 after rising 6.4 in November as new orders, shipments, backlogs and hiring deteriorated. Looking ahead six months, though, survey respondents were optimistic about a pickup in orders.
A third report, from the Labour Department, appeared to buttress the slower-growth scenario as new claims for unemployment pay last week climbed by 1,000 to 351,000 -- the highest level since July.
"The latest reading on claims indicates, at the very least, moderation in the labour market," said economist Marilyn Schaja of brokerage Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp. in New York.
During October, the politically sensitive deficit with Japan shot up by 30.9 percent to $4.96 billion, the highest level in more than a year since $5 billion in August 1995.
Once again, that made Japan the country responsible for the largest single part of the U.S. trade deficit, barely surpassing the $4.90 billion deficit with China.

Even so, the department noted the monthly deficit with China was up for a seventh straight month, likely aggravating trade tensions with the Asian trade giant as imports from it hit a record $5.8 billion.

The department said the key reason for the escalating deficit with Japan was higher imports of cars and parts, partly coinciding with a new model year as dealers brought restyled cars onto their lots.
But Sohn said the "grossly undervalued" yen also played a role in bolstering Japan's sales in U.S. markets.

As recently as April 1995, the yen was valued at 79.5 to the dollar but touched 114 Thursday, making Japanese products cheaper for U.S. buyers and American cars correspondingly more expensive for foreigners to purchase.

The smaller overall trade gap in October owed much to a ballooning of aircraft exports, which more than doubled in value to $1.75 billion in October from $759 million in September. Department officials said it was the highest monthly value for aircraft exports since they hit $2.1 billion in April 1994.

Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor, on vacation in Hawaii, told reporters by telephone that October's lower deficit "is evidence that the economy is continuing to grow in a sustainable fashion in the fourth quarter."
